title: Approximation and Estimation
summary: When an exam question wants a close value rather than an exact one: rounding with the error kept small, approximating percentages, fractions, squares and roots, breaking a product into round numbers, and using the answer options to decide how rough you can be.
learningObjectives: Round each term of an expression so the errors tend to cancel.
Approximate a percentage-of or fraction-of quickly.
Estimate a square, a square root and a large product.
Use the spacing of the answer options to judge how rough an estimate can be.

blocks.title: What the question asks, and the error budget
blocks.markdown:
An approximation question ends with "...(approximate value)". You are not expected to compute the exact figure — only to get close enough to pick the right option, fast.

The options are usually spaced well apart — 240, 260, 280, 300 rather than 271, 272, 273. **That spacing is your error budget.** Glance at it before computing:

- **Options 3 per cent or more apart:** round freely to the nearest 10 or a clean fraction.
- **Options within 1 to 2 per cent:** round more carefully, and keep a running note of whether your estimate is above or below the true value.
- **Two options survive:** compute only the borderline term more exactly to break the tie, rather than redoing the whole line.

Never compute the exact answer to an approximation question — it wastes the time the question is designed to save.

blocks.title: Round so the errors cancel
blocks.markdown:
- **Round each number to something easy**, usually to the nearest 10, 100 or a clean fraction.
- **Balance the direction.** If you round one term up, try to round another down, so the errors partly cancel. In a sum, rounding 4,987 up to 5,000 (plus 13) is fine if another term is rounded down by a similar amount.
- **In a product or quotient, small percentage errors matter, not absolute ones.** Rounding 24.8 to 25 is a 0.8 per cent change; rounding 4,987 to 5,000 is a 0.26 per cent change. Both are safe when the options differ by 3 per cent or more.
- **Do the exact arithmetic only on the rounded numbers**, which are chosen to be easy.
searchKeywords: round each number to nearest ten hundred
round one up one down errors cancel

blocks.title: Percentages and fractions
blocks.markdown:
- **Round the percentage to a friendly fraction:** 19.03 per cent is close to 1/5, 12.4 per cent to 1/8, 33.1 per cent to 1/3, 63.8 per cent to 5/8, 42.9 per cent to 3/7.
- **Round the base to a multiple of the fraction's denominator:** for 1/8 of 2,015, round 2,015 to 2,016 so it divides by 8 cleanly.
- **Split an awkward percentage:** 27 per cent of 640 is 25 per cent (160) plus 2 per cent (about 13), roughly 173.
- **Chain percentages as multipliers:** a 21 per cent rise then a 19 per cent fall is about 1.2 times 0.8, that is 0.96 — a 4 per cent fall.
searchKeywords: round percentage to a friendly fraction
round base to a multiple of the denominator

blocks.title: Squares, roots and products
blocks.markdown:
- **Squares:** for a number ending in 5, n5 squared is n times (n plus 1), then "25" appended — 35 squared is 3 times 4 = 12, so 1,225. For others, use the nearest round number and the identity: 68 squared is (70 minus 2) squared, about 4,900 minus 280, so roughly 4,624.
- **Square roots:** locate the nearest perfect squares and interpolate. The square root of 2,400 lies between 48 (2,304) and 49 (2,401); it is very near 49.
- **Cube roots:** locate the nearest perfect cubes — the cube root of 5,900 is just under 18, since 18 cubed is 5,832.
- **Products:** decompose to round numbers. 216 times 48 is 216 times 50 minus 216 times 2, that is 10,800 minus 432, equal to 10,368.
searchKeywords: square of a number ending in 5
estimate square root by interpolation between perfect squares

blocks.title: Worked example: a messy expression
blocks.markdown:
**Approximate 4,987 divided by 24.8, plus 19.03 per cent of 2,016.**

First term: round to 5,000 divided by 25, which is 200.

Second term: 19.03 per cent is close to 0.19; 0.19 times 2,016 is about 383.

Estimate: 200 plus 383, which is about **583**.

The true value is 4,987 divided by 24.8 (about 201.1) plus 383.6, which is about 584.7 — well within the spacing of a normal option set, so 585 is the choice.

blocks.title: Worked example: percentage of a number
blocks.markdown:
**Approximate 37.9 per cent of 1,203.**

37.9 per cent is very close to 38 per cent, and to the fraction 3/8 (which is 37.5 per cent).

Using 0.38: 0.38 times 1,200 is 456.

The true value is 0.379 times 1,203, which is about **456**. Either the decimal round or the 3/8 route lands on it.

blocks.title: Worked example: a square root
blocks.markdown:
**Approximate the square root of 2,400.**

The nearest perfect squares are 48 squared, which is 2,304, and 49 squared, which is 2,401.

2,400 is only 1 below 2,401, so the root is just under 49.

Interpolating: 48 plus (2,400 minus 2,304) divided by (2,401 minus 2,304), that is 48 plus 96/97, which is about **48.99**.

So the square root of 2,400 is about 49.0.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Rounding everything the same way.** Rounding four terms all up can push a sum well past the right option. Balance the directions.
- **Rounding too hard for close options.** Check the option spacing first.
- **Computing the exact answer.** The question is designed so you do not need to.
- **Losing track of a decimal place** when rounding 24.8 to 25 or 0.190 to 0.19.
- **Approximating a percentage to the wrong fraction:** 27 per cent is nearer 3/11 than 1/4; when in doubt, split it as 25 per cent plus a bit.
- **Interpolating a root the wrong way** — the estimate should sit between the two whole roots, nearer the closer perfect square.
searchKeywords: rounding too hard for close options

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- Read the option spacing; it is your error budget. Never compute the exact value.
- Round each term to something easy, and round one up, one down, so errors cancel. In products and quotients, percentage error is what counts.
- Percentages: round to a friendly fraction, round the base to a multiple of its denominator, split awkward ones as 25 per cent plus a bit, chain as multipliers.
- Squares: n5 squared is n(n+1) then "25"; otherwise use the nearest round number and an identity. Roots: interpolate between the two nearest perfect squares (or cubes).
- Products: decompose into round numbers, for example x times 50 minus x times 2.
- If two options survive, compute only the borderline term more exactly.

flashcards.front: In an approximation question, what tells you how rough you can be?
flashcards.back: The spacing between the answer options. Options 3%+ apart → round freely; options within 1–2% → round carefully and track whether you are above or below the true value.

flashcards.front: Why round one term up and another down?
flashcards.back: So the rounding errors partly cancel and the total error stays small. Rounding every term the same way can push a sum past the right option.
flashcards.explanation: In products/quotients, watch percentage error, not absolute.

flashcards.front: Approximate 19.03% of a number — what is the fast route?
flashcards.back: Treat 19% as 1/5 (or 0.19). Round the base to a multiple of 5 if it helps.

flashcards.front: Fast square of a number ending in 5, e.g. 35²?

flashcards.back: Between 48² = 2304 and 49² = 2401. 2400 is 1 below 2401, so ≈ 48.99, essentially 49.

flashcards.explanation: Turn one factor into a round number, then correct.

flashcards.front: Two options survive your estimate. What now?
flashcards.back: Compute only the one borderline term more exactly to break the tie — don't redo the whole expression.
flashcards.explanation: Preserves the time the estimate saved.
